study_identification_part.si4_title: Mapping the Heterogeneous Phenotype of Schizophrenia and Bipolar Disorder Using Normative Models

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To investigate the degree to which case-control analyses disguise interindividual differences in brain structure among patients with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder and to map the brain alterations linked to these disorders at the level of individual patients using normative modeling.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-score (|z| > 2.6 as extreme, corresponding to P < .005); Percentage of extreme positive and negative deviating voxels relative to total intracerebral voxels
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper explicitly defines the deviation metric as z-scores normalized by the uncertainty of prediction, with a threshold of |z| > 2.6 (P < .005) for extreme deviations. The percentage of extreme deviations across voxels was used as the primary outcome measure.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: Thus, we were able to statistically quantify deviations from the normative model with regional specificity by computing a z score for each voxel that reflected the difference between the predicted volume and the true volume normalized by the uncertainty of the prediction... The threshold for individual deviation maps was established at |z| > 2.6 (ie, P < .005), and extreme positive and extreme negative deviations from the normative model were defined based on this threshold... All extreme deviations were combined into scores that represented the percentage of extreme positive and negative deviating voxels for each participant, expressed relative to the total number of intracerebral voxels.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group comparisons using χ² tests (Bonferroni-Holm corrected) for percentage of extreme deviations between diagnostic groups; Permutation Analysis of Linear Models (PALM) with t-tests for mean group-level deviation maps, using z = ±2.6 (P < .005) threshold and threshold-free cluster enhancement with modality correction for multiple comparisons; Voxelwise overlap analysis to assess spatial extent of extreme deviations across individuals; Linear regressions (Bonferroni-Holm corrected for 12 comparisons within each disorder and modality) testing associations between percentage of extreme deviations and age, disease duration, and cognitive performance (verbal learning/memory, processing speed, working memory, executive functioning); Post-hoc regression analyses to test potential confounding effects of image quality, medication load, and substance abuse on percentage of extreme deviations; Alternative FDR-corrected analyses at individual level using Benjamini-Hochberg procedure; Supplementary analyses using FreeSurfer-derived cortical thickness and surface area to verify findings
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: At the individual level, deviations from the normative model were frequent in both schizophrenia and bipolar disorder but highly heterogeneous, with overlap of more than 2% among patients observed in only a few brain loci, primarily in frontal, temporal, and cerebellar regions, despite robust group-level differences.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Patients with schizophrenia showed significantly reduced gray matter in frontal regions, cerebellum, and temporal cortex on average, while patients with bipolar disorder had mean deviations primarily in cerebellar regions. However, at the individual level, extreme deviations (|z| > 2.6) were highly heterogeneous: in gray matter, patients with schizophrenia had 0.9% of voxels with extreme negative deviations compared to 0.23% in healthy controls (P < .001) and 0.24% in bipolar disorder (P < .001). Healthy individuals had more extreme positive deviations (1.08%) than schizophrenia (0.78%, P = .001) or bipolar disorder (0.79%, P = .001). Similar patterns were observed in white matter. Spatial overlap analysis revealed that only a few brain loci (primarily frontal, temporal, and cerebellar) showed extreme deviations in more than 2% of patients with the same diagnosis. The proportion of alterations was associated with diagnosis and, within clinical groups, with cognitive performance (processing speed and executive functioning in bipolar disorder) and disease duration (positive white matter deviations in schizophrenia), but not with age. Supplementary analyses using cortical thickness and pial area measures confirmed these findings, showing that extreme deviations were principally attributable to cortical thinning. The study found minor associations between image quality and negative gray matter deviations in schizophrenia, and between substance abuse and negative deviations, but diagnostic effects remained significant after controlling for these factors.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The study design does not permit strong inferences about confounding variables; medication effects were tested but the study was not designed to detect them (cross-sectional design, no random assignment, almost all patients medicated, no plasma concentration measures); image quality measures are crude; substance abuse measures are relatively crude and causality cannot be inferred; single-site study limits generalizability
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: A limitation of this study is that it does not permit strong inferences about the degree to which certain confounding variables may have influenced our findings. We did not find evidence of confounding effects of medication but found minor associations between overall image quality and substance abuse with negative deviations in gray matter for schizophrenia... However, the measures that we used to assess this effect are crude, and our design does not permit inferences about the direction of causality (eg, patients with greater severity may move more in the scanner and be more prone to drug abuse).

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study used a fixed statistical threshold (|z| > 2.6, P < .005) for each participant individually rather than controlling FDR separately for each participant, to maintain sensitivity to overall shifts in deviation distributions. Alternative FDR-corrected analyses (Benjamini-Hochberg) were performed and led to identical conclusions. The study created individualized deviation maps and calculated voxelwise overlap to quantify heterogeneity. Supplementary analyses using FreeSurfer cortical thickness and pial area measures replicated the main VBM findings, confirming that extreme deviations were principally due to cortical thinning. The study emphasizes that the lack of substantial overlap among patients provides strong evidence of biological heterogeneity and challenges the concept of the 'average patient' in psychiatry.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a landmark paper in normative modeling for psychiatry, demonstrating extreme biological heterogeneity at the individual level despite robust group-level differences. The study recruited participants from the Thematically Organized Psychosis (TOP) study in Oslo, Norway, from October 2004 to October 2012, with data reanalysis in 2017-2018. All scans were acquired on a single 1.5T Siemens MAGNETOM Sonata scanner using MPRAGE sequences with specific parameters (TR=2730ms, TE=3.93ms, TI=1000ms). Two T1-weighted scans per participant were averaged after rigid registration to improve SNR. Patients were diagnosed using SCID for DSM-IV. The schizophrenia spectrum group (n=218) includes pure schizophrenia (n=163), schizoaffective disorder (n=33), and schizophreniform disorder (n=22). Mean education levels were: healthy controls 14±2.3 years, bipolar disorder 13.57±2.3 years, schizophrenia 12.88±2.6 years. Disease duration (days since diagnosis): bipolar disorder 285.5±352.2, schizophrenia 232.2±330.6. PANSS scores indicated more severe symptoms in schizophrenia than bipolar disorder. Medication use varied: antipsychotics (bipolar 38.9%, schizophrenia 79.1%), lithium (bipolar 18.4%, schizophrenia 1.2%), antiepileptics (bipolar 43.2%, schizophrenia 28.8%), antidepressants (bipolar 27.4%, schizophrenia 52.7%). The normative model showed global gray matter decrease from age 20-70, particularly in frontal and cerebellar regions, with largest decreases in frontal areas for both sexes. White matter showed both decreases and increases across the adult lifespan. The study provides histograms showing the distribution of deviating voxels is sharply peaked, slightly asymmetric with heavy tails, indicating most participants have relatively few but widespread deviations. The paper argues this extreme heterogeneity explains why biomarker discovery and multivariate pattern classification have had limited success in psychiatry, and suggests biological strata may be smaller than previously anticipated.
